gold.display: The angles of a quadrilateral are \(x\), \(2x\), \(3x\) and \(90^\circ\). Find the largest angle.

bronze.label: Together: your first one

steps.say: First the triangle. The three angles add to 180°. Add the two you know:

steps.done: That is the triangle fact: three angles make 180°.

steps.say: Now a and b sit on a straight line, which is 180°.

bronze.display: In a triangle the angles are \(35^\circ\), \(85^\circ\) and \(a\). The angle \(a\) then sits on a straight line next to angle \(b\). Find \(a\) and \(b\).

steps.say: Use the interior-angle-sum formula \((n - 2) \times 180\) with \(n = 12\). First n − 2:

steps.done: That is the total of all 12 interior angles.

steps.say: For a REGULAR polygon every angle is equal, so divide the sum by 12:
Check with the exterior angle. Each exterior = 360 ÷ 12 = 30, and interior + exterior = 180.
steps.done: Both routes give 150°, so it checks.

opener.label: Before any rules

steps.say: One slice is 120° and the next is 150°. The three slices fill the whole pizza, and once round a full circle is 360°.
steps.hint: The three slices fill 360°. Take away 120 and 150.

steps.say: Now picture a fresh pizza cut into 4 equal slices from the centre. Every slice is the same size.

Those totals are the first angle facts: angles that meet at a point always add to 360° (a full turn), and angles on a straight line (a half pizza) add to 180°. Every question here is really just filling a known total.

steps: Spot which angle fact fits the figure (straight line, point, triangle, parallel lines or polygon).
Write the total that those angles must make.
Subtract the known angles, or solve the equation, to find the unknown.
State the reason, e.g. angles on a straight line, alternate angles.
method_card.title: Angle Facts & Properties
method_card.content:
Straight line = 180°. At a point = 360°. Vertically opposite angles are equal. Triangle = 180°, quadrilateral = 360°.

Parallel lines: alternate (Z) equal, corresponding (F) equal, co-interior (C) add to 180°.

Polygon: interior angles sum to \((n-2)\times180^\circ\); each exterior angle of a regular polygon = \(360^\circ\div n\); interior + exterior = 180°.
method_card.example:
Find the interior angle of a regular pentagon.

Sum = \((5 - 2) \times 180 = 540^\circ\). Each angle = \(540 \div 5 = 108^\circ\).

steps: When angles are given as expressions, add them and set the total equal to the correct sum, for example 3x + 4x + 5x = 180 in a triangle.
Solve for the letter, then substitute back to find the angle actually asked for, which is often not x itself.
For polygon problems, link the two facts: interior + exterior = 180° and exterior = 360° ÷ n, then solve.
gold.title: Gold: algebra and multi-step angles

example.question: A triangle has angles 2x, 3x and 40°. Find the largest angle.

steps: Learn the totals. Angles on a straight line add to 180°, angles at a point add to 360°, angles in a triangle add to 180°, and vertically opposite angles are equal.
Pick the fact that matches the figure, then subtract the angles you know from the total.
If an angle repeats, collect it: two equal x angles plus the rest equals the total. In an isosceles triangle the two base angles are equal.
bronze.title: Bronze: basic angle facts

steps.label: Rule
steps.content: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.

example.question: Angles on a straight line are 110° and x. Find x.

steps: With parallel lines: alternate angles (Z) are equal, corresponding angles (F) are equal, and co-interior angles (C) add to 180°.
For a polygon with n sides the interior angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360° ÷ n, and interior + exterior = 180°.
To find n from an exterior angle, divide: n = 360 ÷ exterior angle.
silver.title: Silver: parallel lines and polygons

example.question: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon.

gold.display: The interior angle of a regular polygon is \(156^\circ\). How many sides?

misconceptions.message: 24 is the exterior angle (180 − 156). Divide 360 by it: 360 ÷ 24 = 15 sides.
Do not divide 360 by the interior angle. Find the exterior angle first: 180 − 156 = 24°.

gold.hint: Around the point the three angles add to 360. Subtract both polygon interior angles.
gold.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 170' role="img" aria-label="A regular pentagon and a regular hexagon meet at a point; their interior angles 108 and 120 degrees and the gap x" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='188.0' y2='92.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='99.0' y2='27.3' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='74.5' y2='142.5' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='92' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='142.0' y='65.7' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>108°</text><text x='83.4' y='88.2' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>120°</text><text x='135.2' y='130.2' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>x</text></svg>A regular pentagon and a regular hexagon share a side and meet at a point, with angle \(x\) in the gap between them. Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: 48° comes from the exterior angles. Around the point use the interior angles: 360 − 108 − 120 = 132°.
Do not subtract the two interior angles from each other. Around the point: 360 − 108 − 120 = 132°.

gold.hint: Alternate angles are equal. Set 3x + 10 = 5x − 20 and solve.
gold.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 150' role="img" aria-label="Two parallel lines cut by a transversal with alternate angles 3x plus 10 and 5x minus 20" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='20.0' y1='42.0' x2='220.0' y2='42.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='20.0' y1='116.0' x2='220.0' y2='116.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M116,42 l7,-4 M116,42 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><path d='M116,116 l7,-4 M116,116 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><line x1='72.0' y1='132.0' x2='178.0' y2='28.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='42' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><circle cx='90' cy='116' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><text x='176.0' y='36.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>3x+10</text><text x='74.0' y='131.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>5x−20</text></svg>Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is \(3x + 10\) and its alternate angle is \(5x - 20\). Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: 55 is the size of the angle (3(15) + 10). The question asks for x, which is 15.
These are alternate angles (equal), not co-interior. Set 3x + 10 = 5x − 20.

gold.hint: Interior + exterior = 180. Write 8e + e = 180, find e, then 360 ÷ e.
gold.display: A regular polygon has interior angles 8 times its exterior angles. How many sides?

misconceptions.message: 20 is the exterior angle (e). The number of sides is 360 ÷ 20 = 18.
Interior is 8 times exterior, so 8e + e = 180, giving e = 20° and 18 sides.

gold.hint: At each vertex the interior and exterior angle together make a straight line.
gold.display: To prove the exterior angles of any polygon sum to \(360^\circ\), which fact is used?

misconceptions.message: Angles at a point (360°) is the result you are proving, not the fact you build from. Each interior + exterior = 180°.
The proof does not use the triangle angle sum. It uses interior + exterior = 180° at every vertex.

bronze.hint: Angles on a straight line add to 180. Take 130 away from 180.
bronze.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 140' role="img" aria-label="A straight line with an angle of 130 degrees and an unknown angle x on it" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='25.0' y1='112.0' x2='215.0' y2='112.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='112.0' x2='69.9' y2='52.2' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='112' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='138.6' y='72.1' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>130°</text><text x='81.7' y='95.1' fill='currentColor' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>x</text></svg>Angles on a straight line: \(x\) and \(130^\circ\). Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 360°. x = 180 − 130 = 50°.
These two angles are supplementary (they add to 180°), they are not equal.

bronze.hint: Vertically opposite angles are always equal.
bronze.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 176' role="img" aria-label="Two straight lines crossing, one angle is 72 degrees and its vertically opposite angle is unknown" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='28.0' y1='92.0' x2='212.0' y2='92.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='148.4' y1='4.5' x2='91.6' y2='179.5' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='92' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='157.2' y='65.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>72°</text><text x='82.8' y='122.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>?</text></svg>Vertically opposite angles: one is \(72^\circ\). What is the other?

misconceptions.message: Vertically opposite angles are equal, not supplementary. The answer is 72°.
Do not halve it. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so the answer is 72°.

bronze.hint: Angles in a triangle add to 180. Subtract both known angles.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAngles in a triangle: \(55^\circ\), \(80^\circ\) and \(x\). Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: Angles in a triangle add to 180°, not 360°. x = 180 − 55 − 80 = 45°.
135° is the two known angles added. Subtract them from 180° instead: x = 45°.

bronze.hint: Angles at a point add to 360. Subtract the two known angles.
bronze.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 170' role="img" aria-label="Three angles meeting at a point: 90 degrees, 150 degrees and an unknown angle" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='188.0' y2='92.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='120.0' y2='24.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='92.0' x2='86.0' y2='150.9' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='92' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='146.4' y='69.6' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>90°</text><text x='83.9' y='86.3' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>150°</text><text x='138.7' y='128.4' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>?</text></svg>Three angles at a point are \(90^\circ\), \(150^\circ\) and \(x\). Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: 240° is the two known angles added. Take that from 360°: x = 360 − 240 = 120°.
Angles at a point add to 360°, not 180°.

bronze.hint: The two base angles are equal. Share what is left after the top angle between them.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyAn isosceles triangle has a top angle of \(40^\circ\). Find each base angle.

misconceptions.message: 140° is the two base angles together. They are equal, so divide by 2: 70°.
A base angle is not equal to the top angle. 180 − 40 = 140, then divide by 2 to get 70°.

bronze.display: What is the angle sum of a quadrilateral?

misconceptions.message: 180° is a triangle. A quadrilateral has 4 sides: (4 − 2) × 180 = 360°.
540° is a pentagon (5 sides). A quadrilateral has angle sum 360°.

bronze.hint: A right angle is 90. Subtract 90 and 35 from 180.
bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA right angle, \(35^\circ\) and \(x\) are in a triangle. Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: The right angle is 90°. x = 180 − 90 − 35 = 55°.
Angles in a triangle add to 180°, not 360°.

bronze.hint: There are two equal x angles. Set up 2x + 60 = 180.
bronze.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 138' role="img" aria-label="A straight line split into three angles: x, x and 60 degrees" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='22.0' y1='118.0' x2='218.0' y2='118.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='118.0' x2='167.0' y2='50.8' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120.0' y1='118.0' x2='92.0' y2='40.9' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='118' r='3' fill='currentColor'/><text x='164.6' y='95.3' fill='currentColor' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>x</text><text x='127.0' y='68.5' fill='currentColor' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>x</text><text x='79.0' y='89.3' fill='currentColor' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>60°</text></svg>Angles on a straight line: \(x\), \(x\) and \(60^\circ\). Find \(x\).

misconceptions.message: There are two x angles. Use 2x + 60 = 180, which gives x = 60°.
Angles on a straight line add to 180°, not 360°.

silver.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 150' role="img" aria-label="Two parallel lines cut by a transversal, one alternate angle is 65 degrees" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='20.0' y1='42.0' x2='220.0' y2='42.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='20.0' y1='116.0' x2='220.0' y2='116.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M116,42 l7,-4 M116,42 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><path d='M116,116 l7,-4 M116,116 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><line x1='72.0' y1='132.0' x2='178.0' y2='28.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='42' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><circle cx='90' cy='116' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><text x='176.0' y='36.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>65°</text><text x='74.0' y='131.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>?</text></svg>Parallel lines cut by a transversal. One alternate angle is \(65^\circ\). Find the other.

misconceptions.message: Alternate angles are equal, not supplementary. The answer is 65°.
Alternate angles are equal (both 65°), they do not add to 90°.

silver.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 150' role="img" aria-label="Two parallel lines cut by a transversal, one co-interior angle is 110 degrees" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><line x1='20.0' y1='42.0' x2='220.0' y2='42.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='20.0' y1='116.0' x2='220.0' y2='116.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M116,42 l7,-4 M116,42 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><path d='M116,116 l7,-4 M116,116 l7,4' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.4' fill='none'/><line x1='72.0' y1='132.0' x2='178.0' y2='28.0' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='42' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><circle cx='90' cy='116' r='2.5' fill='currentColor'/><text x='140.0' y='58.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>110°</text><text x='74.0' y='108.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>?</text></svg>Co-interior angle with a parallel line: one angle is \(110^\circ\). Find the other.

misconceptions.message: Co-interior angles add to 180°, they are not equal. 180 − 110 = 70°.
Co-interior angles sum to 180°, not 360°.

silver.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 180' role="img" aria-label="A regular hexagon" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><polygon points='120.0,22.0 68.0,52.0 68.0,112.0 120.0,142.0 172.0,112.0 172.0,52.0' fill='#34d399' fill-opacity='0.16' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='120.0' y='168.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>regular hexagon</text></svg>Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.

misconceptions.message: A hexagon has 6 sides, not 5. (6 − 2) × 180 = 720°.

silver.display: Each exterior angle of a regular polygon is \(40^\circ\). How many sides?

misconceptions.message: 40 is the exterior angle, not the number of sides. Sides = 360 ÷ 40 = 9.
Divide 360 by the exterior angle, not the interior angle.

silver.display: <svg viewBox='0 0 240 180' role="img" aria-label="A regular decagon with ten sides" style='max-width:250px;width:100%;height:auto;font-family:Inter,sans-serif'><polygon points='120.0,22.0 84.7,33.5 62.9,63.5 62.9,100.5 84.7,130.5 120.0,142.0 155.3,130.5 177.1,100.5 177.1,63.5 155.3,33.5' fill='#34d399' fill-opacity='0.16' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='2'/><text x='120.0' y='168.0' fill='currentColor' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='normal'>regular decagon</text></svg>Find each interior angle of a regular decagon (10 sides).

misconceptions.message: 36° is the exterior angle (360 ÷ 10). The interior angle is 180 − 36 = 144°.
A decagon has 10 sides. Interior = (10 − 2) × 180 ÷ 10 = 144°.

silver.display: An exterior angle of a regular polygon is \(30^\circ\). What is the interior angle?

misconceptions.message: Interior and exterior angles add to 180°, they are not equal. 180 − 30 = 150°.
Interior and exterior angles add to 180°, not 360°.

silver.hint: Add the parts: 3x + 4x + 5x = 180. Solve for x, then work out 5x.
silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA triangle has angles \(3x\), \(4x\) and \(5x\). Find the largest angle.

misconceptions.message: 60° is the middle angle (4x). The largest is 5x = 75°.
45° is the smallest angle (3x). The largest is 5x = 75°.
